# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

- F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate takes its bound where every argument is below it.** It builds P-48. A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes (F-137); where some argument is not below its bound, it takes the arguments' join. A type parameter that the declared parameter types mention only in function domains, an odd number of arrows deep and never inside a static argument, as `T` in `g: T -> ZZ32`, is bounded by the arguments only from above. Where nothing bounds it from below, it takes the meet of its declared bound and the bounds that the arguments place on it. An F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143). A reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument fixes its big operator's parameter by the declared type of its value, else by its elements' join (F-228). That rule is the coordinator's call. Two more rules are defaults of the walk-instance rung's decision record. First, a parameter that only another fixed parameter's bound mentions takes that parameter's instance, not its own bound: `ap[\T, A extends T\](a: A)` gives `T` the type of `a` (D3, row 592). Second, a lone one whose bound mentions a static parameter has the arguments' supertypes among its candidates, and so takes their narrowest common supertype, never its bound (D5). Defects, each with an expected failure: two bounds that walk cannot meet (row 591); a bound only from above that mentions another static parameter, which keeps `Bottom` (walk's `BottomType`) (row 612); two upper bounds from two function arguments that walk cannot meet, which fail the call (row 616); a parameter that only the result of a function expression with no declared return type fixes, which takes `Bottom` (row 587); a generic passed over at dispatch when its arguments have several minimal common supertypes (row 589), whose repair changes which declaration runs, the curator's to decide. Gated by `tests/Infer*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/REPORT.md` section 2 and its `decision-record.md` section 2; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 1; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-meet/REPORT.md` section 1.

- F-143 **Under walk, a type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left open.** Such a bound is an F-bound, as in `mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\]()`. The open type, printed `OPEN`, is below every type, and every value matches it. A reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument is first instantiated by its declared type or by its elements' join (F-228). So the open parameter reaches one only where neither fixes it: an empty `SUM` or `PROD` that no declared type directs, which takes `ZZ32`'s identity whatever its body's type (row 716), or a clause form whose declared type or join does not fit the bound (F-228). A call such as `mk()` also leaves it open. Where overloads are compared, a tuple, arrow or generic type that holds the open type admits no more than it would at `BottomType`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` does not take `(1, 2)`, though a lone `one(x: (T,T))` does (row 663, contested). In a probe by the rung's skeptic, the agent that checks a rung's work after its worker, a method declared over `T` in an object whose `T` stayed open was the most specific one, and so was chosen for every argument; no gated test holds this. A list comprehension written at such an open parameter, as `<|[\T\] x | x <- xs |>`, ends in `CastError` at its unwrap's cast, `cast[\CovariantCollection[\T\]\](cc)` (`Library/List.fss:179`), and so does `List`'s range subscript at a stride other than 1 on a list of that open element type, since the subscript writes `[\E\]` (row 825, contested). Gated by `tests/InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk.fss`, `OpenTupleDispatchWalk.fss` and `OpenParameterListComprehensionWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-open-param/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 11; its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3, finding 3 (the probe); `compile-ladder/rung-body-arguments/SKEPTIC.md` section 3.

- F-78 **The compiled checker instantiates a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes at the intersection of its upper bounds, never `BottomType`, and tries a call by subtyping without the expected type first.** It builds P-48 and P-49. Where the call has an expected type, its attempts come in this order: subtyping without the expected type, kept when its result converts to it; subtyping with the expected type; coercion with it; and coercion without it. The second lets a call whose untyped function argument only the expected type fixes type-check, since the coercion attempt cannot check such an argument (row 507). P-49 decides the first and the third; the second and the fourth are an agent's choice, the instance-bound rung's (its decision record, D4). An argument of intersection type fixes a parameter at the whole intersection, not at one conjunct (row 541). The run time has no class for an intersection type, so such an instance dies as it loads (row 559). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferResultOnly*` and `InferContextKeepsFit`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 7; the order, by reading, `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/decision-record.md`, D4, and `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:733-737`.

- **Evidence.** P-157, P-146, F-277, F-225, row 804 (open at `aff478ca5`); for the scope, F-281, F-81, F-245 and row 584 (fixed `108ab82d6`); `compiler_tests/ExclusionVectorScalarBlock` (typecheck), `XXXExclusionSelfTypeSharedLeft` and `...Right` (refused), `tests/XXXExclusionVectorScalarWalk.fss`; `compile-ladder/rung-self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 4, and `SKEPTIC.md`, `SkVecRun` (compiled, each call runs its declaration); `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:264-269` and `:2701-2711`.

## Case 22: an index parameter's bound, and a function over `Index` beside one over a pair

- **Trap.** An unbounded type parameter is the norm, as in Java and Scala, and the model program's own files declare their index parameters so. No trait type holds a tuple: the Working Draft says that "every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type" and that "a tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than `Any`" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:215-216`, `:272-273`). The pretraining quiz's priors on tuples are weak (§2, "`Any` does not include tuples", graded wrong in the audit, B.2). A worker failure: microGPT's helpers declare the index parameter unbounded (`explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi:15-21`, `explorations/apl/mg/FlatArrays2.fsi:68-73` and `:126`, `explorations/apl/mg/AplMg.fsi:41`), and the team's `UniformDistribution` had to take the bound (`Library/Random.fsi:260`).
- **Expected.**
  - (a) `tanh[\T extends Number, I extends Index\](a: Array[\T,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\]`. Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index` (`Indexed[\E, I extends Index\]`), so `Array[\T,I\]` at an unbounded `I` is ill-formed to the checker: "Ill-formed type: Array[\RR64,I\] The static argument I does not satisfy the corresponding bound Index." The bounded form is accepted. Walk checks no static types, so it runs the unbounded form, and the quick check passing proves nothing. The compiled path first reads the declaration after the switch-over: until then it compiles against the compiler's prelude, which has no arrays, and the model program's components stop at name resolution.
  - (b) The pair is not valid. A tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index` (P-156), and `Index` excludes a tuple type only where one of its element types excludes `Index`. `Cell` does not, so for `object G extends { Cell, Index }` the pair `(G, G)` lies in both domains. Neither domain lies inside the other, and no declaration covers their meet, so the Meet Rule refuses the pair. The checker refuses it, with the interpreter's library, "Invalid overloading of place"; before the switch-over the compiled path does not get that far, since the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`. Walk loads the pair (row 806) and, at the overlap, runs `place(x: Index)`. Change: `trait Cell excludes { Index }`, row 806's workaround. Then `(Cell, Cell)` excludes `Index`, and the pair is valid.
- **Scope.** `ZZ32` and every tuple of `ZZ32` are `Index` types, so every array of the model program fits the bound. `Index` extends only `Any`, so a tuple of indices is still no `Object`, and `()` is no `Index`. The checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, as `place((i, j))` would be at a lone `place(x: Index)` (row 805); a typed variable for the tuple works.
